chapters.name: The supplier's call
chapters.blurb: Prices, deliveries and who you trust to bring things on time.
chapters.fact: A supplier you pay on time and talk to honestly will often protect you in a shortage. Price is one line on the invoice; reliability is the rest.

chapters.name: Over the counter
chapters.blurb: What customers say, ask for and quietly decide.
chapters.fact: Most unhappy customers never complain; they just stop coming. A fast, fair answer to the few who do is cheap advertising.

chapters.name: The team
chapters.blurb: Small moments with the people who do the work.
chapters.fact: People rarely leave over one thing. They leave over a run of small ones nobody answered.

chapters.name: Small money
chapters.blurb: Offers, tips and little bets with real stakes.
chapters.fact: Anything that promises a sure return for no effort is priced that way because someone else is carrying the risk. Find out who.

chapters.name: In the papers
chapters.blurb: Something you read that might matter next week.
chapters.fact: News moves a business in two steps: first what happened, then what everyone does about it. The second step is where you have a choice.

chapters.name: Down the street
chapters.blurb: Other businesses, other owners, and the local scene.
chapters.fact: Competitors are also your best research. Watch what they stop doing as closely as what they start.

items.t: A new rep rings
items.s: A rep from a supplier you have never used rings {co} with an introductory price. The samples look fine, and the contract is for a year.

o.r: The trial order came on time and the price held. You saved a little on the first month and kept your usual supplier as well.
Your usual supplier heard you had been approached and quietly held its price. Nothing changed, which is sometimes the whole point.
The introductory month was good. Then the deliveries slipped and the price crept up.
o.rb: The first deliveries were late and the price crept up after the introductory month. A year is a long time to be tied to that.

items.t: Short delivery
items.s: A delivery arrives about a quarter short, and the driver shrugs. The paperwork says it is all there.

o.r: The supplier apologised, sent the rest the next day and took something off the invoice. They check your orders more carefully now.

o.l: Ask for a credit, keep the goods
o.r: A credit note came through without fuss. You kept trading and nobody lost face.

o.h: Easy, but they notice you do not check
o.r: Nothing was said, and the next delivery was short again. You will check from now on.

items.t: The invoice is a bit high
items.s: This month's supplier invoice is a few percent above the quote. The rep says it is a fuel surcharge.

o.r: The surcharge turned out to be a mistake on their side. The corrected invoice arrived two days later.
You paid. Next month's invoice carried the same surcharge, as these things tend to.

o.l: Ask for a better price on the next order
o.h: A conversation about the whole account
o.r: They would not drop the surcharge, but they gave you a better price on your next order to keep you happy.

items.t: A discount for ordering in bulk
items.s: Your supplier of consumables (cleaning, napkins, towels, small things that always run out) offers a good discount if {co} orders a quarter's worth at once and pays up front.

o.r: The discount was real and the storeroom is full. It is a little tighter in the bank for a few weeks.
A smaller discount, a smaller bill, and a storeroom you can still walk around in.
Nothing changed. You ran out of napkins once, and somebody went to the shop.

items.t: Last season's lines
items.s: A wholesaler offers {co} a pallet of last season's lines at close to cost. They sell, but not at full price.

o.r: Most of it sold at a modest price during a quiet week. A few pieces are still on the shelf.
o.rb: Half of it is still in the stockroom, and the cash is tied up in it. A lesson in how much storage space costs.

o.r: A few cases went quickly and gave the front of the shop something fresh.
You kept the range clean. A regular said they liked the shop looking the same as always.

items.t: Raw materials may get dearer
items.s: A trade contact says the main raw material may get dearer in a month or two. Nothing is certain.

o.h: Costs money now, may pay off
o.r: The price did go up a little. Your stock was bought before it, so the next few weeks run a touch cheaper.
o.rb: The rumour came to nothing and the price stayed flat. You carry some extra stock you did not need yet.

o.r: You waited. The price moved a little, as prices do.

o.l: Ask your supplier to fix a price
o.r: Your supplier agreed to hold the price for six weeks in return for a steady order.

items.t: An early system upgrade
items.s: The vendor of your core system offers {co} an early upgrade at a reduced rate. It promises faster month-ends and fewer manual fixes.

o.r: The upgrade went in over a quiet weekend. Month-end is a little less painful and the team noticed.
o.rb: The upgrade overran by a day and cost extra in support. It works now, and everyone is a little tired.

o.r: You waited. The next release was already scheduled, and a few more fixes came with it.
The vendor ran a pilot on one process. It worked, and they gave you a small discount for being patient.

items.t: A customer is cross
items.s: A customer of {co} has written a long, angry email about something that really did go wrong.

o.r: They wrote back a short thank-you and said they would give you another go. You could see the little goodwill gesture it took.
They did not reply. The matter is closed, though no one is happier.
They did not come back, and told a friend why.

items.t: A glowing review, a small catch
items.s: A customer left a glowing public review of {co}. One line at the end mentions a long wait.

o.l: Thank them and fix the wait
o.h: A little effort on a real problem
o.r: The thanks was noticed by other readers, and the wait is shorter now.
A tidy reply. A little goodwill, nothing more.
Nothing was said. The review stays up, wait and all.

items.t: A regular asks for a favour
items.s: One of your best customers asks if {co} could do something slightly outside the usual, just for them.

o.r: They were delighted and mentioned it to three friends. It took an afternoon of someone's time.
They paid without complaint and kept coming. A clean arrangement.
They understood, a little less warmly than before.

items.t: The January crowd has not left
items.s: Many of the members who joined in the new year are still coming, but the equipment queue is longer than it was. One member asks if {co} will ever add more machines.

o.r: Evening classes filled up fast, and the machine queue shortened a little.
Two machines arrived and members noticed within a week. The queue still forms at six in the evening, but it moves.
Most were patient. A couple said so on the way out, and one quietly left.

items.t: A long-standing customer is annoyed at a fee
items.s: A customer of twenty years is cross about a fee at {co}. They are not wrong, but the fee is policy.

o.r: They sent a short, grateful note, and mentioned your name to their daughter, who is starting a business.
They accepted the explanation without warmth. The account stays open.

o.l: Waive the fee and review the policy
o.r: The review found two fees nobody could defend. They were dropped, and a few customers noticed.

items.t: A client wants to be squeezed in
items.s: A client of {co} asks to be fitted in outside normal hours. It would make a long day.

o.r: They were grateful and tipped well. Everyone was tired by evening.
They took the next slot with good grace.
They found someone else this week and came back next month.

items.t: A return with no receipt
items.s: A shopper brings back something to {co} without a receipt. It is plausible, and it is also the sort of thing people try on.

o.r: They left pleased and bought something else. The returns book has one more line.
They took the credit and spent it within the month.
They left unhappy and said so in the reviews. The policy stays clean.

items.t: Someone has been late three times
items.s: One of the team at {co} has been late three times this month. They are good at the job.

o.r: It turned out to be a bus timetable. Their start time moved fifteen minutes and the problem went away.
They were on time after that, and noticeably quieter.
Two others noticed it was let go, and one of them started drifting in late as well.

items.t: A good idea from the floor
items.s: One of the team at {co} suggests a small change to how things are done. It looks sensible, and it is not their job to suggest it.

o.r: It worked well enough to keep. The person who suggested it stood a little taller.

o.l: Thank them and think about it
o.r: They never heard back, and have not suggested anything since.
They ran it well, and are now the person people go to with questions.

items.t: Someone hands in a note
items.s: A good member of {co} hands in a month's notice. They have been offered a bit more elsewhere.

o.r: They stayed, and told you honestly it was close. Wages are a little higher.
They left on good terms. They said they would send a friend your way.

o.l: Ask what would make them stay
o.r: It was not the money at all: it was the Saturdays. A rota change kept them.

items.t: A trainer wants to run a class
items.s: One of the trainers at {co} wants to start a small Saturday class of their own. It could bring new faces.

o.r: The class filled to half and grew. New faces mean new members.
They took it well and asked again in a month.
A leaflet and a poster did the work, and the class filled twice over.

items.t: A promising analyst
items.s: A young analyst at {co} has been quietly excellent. A rival firm has been seen taking them to lunch.

o.r: They took the bigger role and the lunch invitations stopped.
They came back with new ideas and a certificate. Several colleagues asked about courses too.
They stayed through the quarter and left after it. The desk has a gap.

items.t: Two people want the same Saturday
items.s: Two of the team at {co} both want the same Saturday off, and only one can have it.

o.l: Split it fairly, a half each
o.r: Both took the half-day with good grace and a nod to each other.
The loser laughed it off. Someone still brings it up now and then.
One of them stayed home and the other went quiet. It passed, slowly.

items.t: A foreman asks for better kit
items.s: The person who runs the floor at {co} asks for a better set of tools, saying the old ones slow everybody down.

o.r: Work moved a touch faster the following week, and the crew noticed you listened.

o.l: Ask for a shortlist and a price
o.r: The shortlist was sensible and the order went in a few days later.

o.l: Say the old ones will do
o.r: The old ones did do. The foreman did not ask again.

items.t: A tip from a friend
items.s: A friend of a friend says a small company they know is about to announce something big. You could put a modest sum of {co}'s spare cash into it. The word is not worth much.

o.r: The company announced something ordinary, and the share price barely moved. You missed nothing.
It went a little well. It could just as easily have gone the other way, and you knew it.
o.rb: It went the other way. A small loss, and a small lesson about tips from friends of friends.

o.r: Nobody could say where it came from. You felt better for asking.

items.t: An offer of a better rate
items.s: Your bank writes to {co} with a new business account that promises lower fees, if you move everything over.

o.r: The move took two weeks of small headaches. The new fees are lower by a hair.

o.l: Ask your own bank to match
o.r: They matched it, a little grudgingly, rather than lose you.
You stayed. The new account was no better than it sounded.

items.t: Some cash sits idle
items.s: A little cash at {co} has been sitting idle for weeks, and you wonder what to do with it.

o.r: An early payment earned a small discount from a supplier who liked the surprise.
You kept it. A cushion is quiet, but it is nice to have.

o.l: Spend it on a little marketing
o.r: A small campaign brought a few new faces through the door.

items.t: A cautious voice at the desk
items.s: A senior colleague at {co} says the loan book has grown quickly and wonders if the team should slow down and recheck a few of the riskier loans.

o.r: Two loans were fixed before they could go wrong. It cost a week of attention.
Growth continued. A few borrowers were late, and the colleague said nothing.
o.rb: A couple of borrowers fell behind, and the colleague nodded gravely. It cost a little, and everyone noticed.

o.r: The book grew a little more slowly. The colleague seemed relieved.

items.t: A card machine rep
items.s: A rep offers {co} a new card terminal with lower fees. The old one works fine, and the new one has a nicer screen.

o.r: The switch was painless. Fees are a touch lower and customers like the new screen.

o.l: Ask your current provider to match
o.r: They matched it with a shrug.
Nothing changed, and the old terminal went on working.

items.t: A marketplace invites you to list
items.s: An online marketplace invites {co} to list its goods or services. It takes a cut of every sale.

o.r: A few sales came through, at a cut that stung a little. New customers, though.
You declined and kept your margins. A competitor listed there.
Slow lines moved at a small discount, and the cut was easy to bear.

items.t: An energy saving quote
items.s: A contractor quotes {co} for work that should trim the energy bill. The payback is a year or two.

o.r: The work was done in a day. The bill will take a few months to show the difference.
A second contractor was cheaper for the same work. You did it with them.
You put it off. The bill came in much as before.

items.t: A wet week ahead
items.s: The forecast promises a wet, cold week. {co} will feel it a little, one way or the other.

o.r: It was quiet, as forecast. A trimmed rota kept costs in line.
The offer brought a few people in from the rain.
The week was a little quiet, the way wet weeks are.

items.t: The central bank holds its breath
items.s: The papers say the central bank may change rates next month. Opinions differ, as they do.

o.r: You read through the loan terms. One was worth a conversation with the bank.
Rates did what they did. You stayed calm.
The accountant's advice was simple: nothing to do yet, but keep an eye on it.

items.t: A story about a competitor
items.s: The local paper runs a friendly story about a competitor of {co}. It is flattering, and slightly irritating.

o.l: Send them a note of congratulations
o.r: They replied warmly. Owners talk, and this one remembers.
The paper ran a short piece on {co}. A few new faces appeared.
You ignored it. The story went away within the week.

items.t: A big event in town
items.s: The papers announce a large event in town next month. {co} will be busy, if it prepares for it.

o.r: The weekend of the event was the busiest you can remember. Preparation paid for itself.

o.l: Add a few extra hands only
o.r: A little extra help kept the queue short. Takings were good.
You carried on. The crowd came, and some walked past because the wait was long.

items.t: A regulator's letter does the rounds
items.s: A regulator has written to firms like {co} about how they treat customers who fall behind. It is not about you, yet.

o.r: You found two letters in need of kinder wording. Customers noticed the new tone.
They said you were fine, with two suggestions.
You waited. The rule arrived with a deadline and a little more homework.

items.t: Everyone is talking about one product
items.s: A product is all over the news, and customers ask {co} if you have it. It may last a month, or a year.

o.r: It sold briskly for a few weeks, then slowed. You sold what you had.
It sold well, then collapsed. You kept some of it in the stockroom for a while.
o.rb: The craze ended sooner than expected, leaving a pile in the stockroom and a bill to match.

o.r: You ignored it. Customers asked a few more times, then stopped.

items.t: A new rule is announced
items.s: The government announces a new rule that touches {co}. Details to follow, in the way details do.

o.r: You found one clause that mattered and acted on it early. The deadline came and went without fuss.
The trade body had a summary, and a friendly adviser.
The details arrived with a short deadline.

items.t: A neighbour asks to compare notes
items.s: The owner of a business next door to {co} asks if you would like to compare notes over a coffee. They are not a competitor.

o.r: You learned about a supplier you had not heard of, and shared one of yours.
A good conversation. You both left with a small idea or two.
They did not ask again for a while.

items.t: A joint promotion
items.s: A nearby business suggests a joint flyer with {co}: each leaflet carries both names. It costs a little each.

o.r: Both businesses saw a few new faces. The flyer was a bit crowded.
A small card at each till did nearly as well.
They went ahead with someone else.

items.t: The shop next door may close
items.s: The shop next door to {co} may be closing. Footfall may change, one way or the other.

o.l: Ask the landlord about the space
o.r: The landlord said it might be re-let to a café. Footfall may rise a little.
The shop stayed open another month.

o.l: Tell the team to expect a change
o.r: The team appreciated the warning.

items.t: A boutique studio opens round the corner
items.s: A small boutique studio is opening round the corner from {co}. It is small, and expensive, and fashionable.

o.l: Offer a taster week to members' friends
o.r: The taster week brought in a few friends and some goodwill. A few joined.
The studio opened. A few members tried it, and most stayed.
A small cut kept the waverers, and cost a little margin.

items.t: A rival's owner invites you to speak
items.s: The head of a rival firm invites {co} to share a panel at a local conference. It is flattering, and it is also advertising for them.

o.r: You spoke well and said little you regretted. Several people introduced themselves afterwards.
Your deputy spoke well and earned a small round of applause.
You declined. The panel went ahead without you.

items.t: A noisy night next door
items.s: A neighbour of {co} has complained about noise or deliveries, politely, once.

o.l: Call round and sort it out
o.r: A cup of tea and a small change of delivery times settled it for good.
They accepted the note, with a slightly clipped tone.
They complained again, to someone higher up.

items.t: A local trade fair
items.s: A local trade fair is coming up, and a stall for {co} costs a modest fee.

o.r: You made a handful of useful contacts, and a few new orders followed.
You picked up a few ideas and some brochures. One was worth a call.
You skipped it. A competitor won a good order there.
